stem: Murthy’s utility isf(√q₁+√q₂),f′>0, for idli and vara; only integer pieces are sold. Initial prices1,2. (a) He bought6 of each. Was this optimal within the same spending? Find the optimum. (b) Next day each item costs1.50. Can he attain the previous day’s optimal utility without spending more?
answer: (a) No; optimum is12 idli and3 vara, costing18. (b) Impossible within18. The best new affordable bundles are(6,6), below the previous optimum’s utility.
solution: Becausef is increasing maximize√q₁+√q₂. The initial order costs18. The continuous first-order ratio givesq₁=4q₂; the budgetq₁+2q₂18 then gives(12,3), already integer and therefore the integer optimum. Its index is3√3≈5.196, above2√6≈4.899 from(6,6). At new equal prices1.50, spending18 permits at most12 pieces in total. Concavity makes their sum of roots largest at equal division(6,6), whose index2√6 remains below3√3. Hence the requested combination of satisfaction and spending is unattainable. At least14 total integer pieces are needed to weakly reach the old index, since even the most balanced13-piece split has√6+√7<3√3;14 balanced pieces cost21. Exact equality is possible with(12,3)or(3,12), costing22.50.
hint: Use monotone transformation, then respect the indivisible-piece budget.
notes: Visual inspection confirms the revised priceRs1.50, rather than1.60. The infeasibility in part(b) follows from the stated data.

stem: Four sisters share farm output equally among those working. Output with1,2,3,4 sisters is1500,2500,3300,4000. Each may instead earn1110 in the city. How many migrate when maximizing(a) individual income,(b) family income?
answer: (a) Two migrate, two remain. (b) Three migrate, one remains.
solution: Farm average incomes are1500,1250,1100,1000. At two farm workers each gets1250>1110 and will stay, while a migrant joining them would get1100<1110, so two on the farm is the individual-choice equilibrium. For family optimization compare total incomes: no farm workers4440; one farm worker1500+3·1110=4830; two2500+2·1110=4720; three3300+1110=4410; four4000. The maximum4830 uses one farm worker and three migrants. Equivalently the first worker’s marginal product1500 exceeds the city wage, while the second’s1000 does not.
hint: Private entrants compare average product; the family compares marginal product.

stem: There are100 competitive firms withq=√x. Derive industry supply if(a) input supply is horizontal at input price10,(b) total input supply is vertical at100 units.
answer: (a) Q=5P, upward sloping. (b) Q100, vertical, with input priceP/2 for positive output priceP.
solution: With input pricew, a firm choosesq to maximizePq−wq², givingq=P/(2w). In(a),w10, so eachq=P/20 and100 firms supplyQ5P. In(b), symmetry and diminishing returns allocate the100 input units equally: eachx1,q1, totalQ100. The firm conditionP/(2√x)=w givesw=P/2, so input price adjusts to the output price while total output remains fixed. Zero-price degeneracies aside, the output supply curve is vertical at100.
hint: First derive input-price-conditional firm supply, then clear the input market.

stem: Industry inverse demand isP=a−Q and aggregate marginal costMC=Q,a>0. Compute monopoly deadweight loss relative to perfect competition with the same marginal-cost curve.
solution: Competition equatesP=MC: a−Q=Q, givingQ_c=a/2. Monopoly equatesMR=a−2Q withMC=Q, givingQ_m=a/3. AtQ_m the demand-minus-cost gap isa−2a/3=a/3. The surplus-loss triangle has widtha/2−a/3=a/6 and heighta/3, soDWL=(1/2)(a/6)(a/3)=a²/36.
hint: Compare marginal willingness to pay with marginal cost over the missing output range.

stem: A farmer owns1000 bushels, with a physical return110 next year for each100 set aside. UtilityW=C₀C₁. (a) Without a capital market find consumption. (b) He can borrow any amount at5% annually only to finance current consumption: find consumption in both years.
answer: (a) C₀500,C₁550. (b) Set aside all1000, borrow11000/21≈523.810 for current consumption; C₀11000/21,C₁550.
solution: (a) With investmentS, C₀1000−S,C₁1.1S; maximizing1.1S(1000−S) givesS500. (b) LetB be borrowing, restricted to consumption, so0≤S≤1000, C₀1000−S+B andC₁1.1S−1.05B. Present-value resources at the borrowing rate areC₀+C₁/1.05=1000+(1.1/1.05−1)S, increasing inS. Thus chooseS1000; this borrowing restriction prevents using loans to plant more than the original stock. ThenC₀B andC₁1100−1.05B. MaximizingB(1100−1.05B) givesB1100/2.1=11000/21, leavingC₁550. Current consumption rises while future consumption stays550. Without the “only current consumption” restriction, unlimited borrowing for a10% physical return against5% financing would create unbounded arbitrage.
hint: Use the borrowing-use restriction and optimize physical investment before consumption timing.
notes: Part(b) continues on PDFpage7, before the question’s start in the supplied scan order.

stem: A small country faces world pricep_w. One domestic producer has increasingMC, sells both at home and abroad, and is protected against imports by tariffT per unit. Show that raisingT cannot lower exports. When are exports constant?
answer: With positive exports total output is fixed byMC=p_w. Higher tariff weakly raises domestic monopoly price, weakly lowers domestic sales and therefore weakly raises exports. Exports are constant once the import-price ceiling is nonbinding.
solution: Because the producer exports at the fixed world price, an extra unit can always earnp_w; interior total productionQ* satisfiesMC(Q*)=p_w, independent ofT. For givenQ*, allocating a unit to the home market instead of exports has opportunity costp_w. The home monopoly therefore chooses its preferred price against domestic demand subject to the import-parity ceilingp_h≤p_w+T. RaisingT relaxes that ceiling: under ordinary downward demand and a single-peaked domestic profit objective, the home price weakly rises toward its unconstrained optimum and home sales weakly fall. Export quantityE=Q*−q_h thus cannot decline. If the ceiling already exceeds the unconstrained domestic monopoly price (MR_h=p_w), further tariff increases do not affecthome sales or exports. More generally unchanged domestic quantity, for example on an inelastic segment, also leaves exports constant.
hint: Exports pin down marginal cost and total production; the tariff changes only the home allocation.
notes: Uses the standard import-parity-price-ceiling and regular domestic-demand interpretation, with positive exports maintained.

stem: There are100 identical competitive firms withq=x and price-taking behaviour in the input market. Derive industry supply if(a) input price is10 at any quantity,(b) aggregate input supply is fixed100.
answer: (a) Horizontal output supply atP10. (b) Vertical supply atQ100, with input price equal toP.
solution: The technology converts one input unit into one output unit. At constant input pricew, profit is(P−w)q. ForP<w supply is0; forP=w any nonnegative output is optimal; forP>w there is no finite unconstrained optimum. Thus a competitive industry with perfectly elastic input supply at10 has horizontal supplyP10. If total input is fixed100 and positive output prices induce its full use, total output must equal100. Input-market competition bidsw up toP, leaving zero per-unit profit; distribution of the input among firms does not affect aggregate output because production is linear.
hint: With constant returns, output supply may be horizontal rather than a single-valued quantity function.

stem: In a simple Keynesian model, private investment increases with aggregate income. Relative to1/MPS, what is the autonomous-spending multiplier?
answer: B:Greater than1/MPS under the stable-equilibrium condition.
solution: With savingS=sY and investmentI=I₀+vY,v>0, equilibrium gives(s−v)Y=I₀. The multiplier is1/(s−v), greater than1/s when0<v<s. Ifv≥s, the standard stable multiplier comparison fails; the conventional question implicitly assumes stability.
hint: Induced investment adds a second positive expenditure feedback.
notes: Assumes the marginal propensity to save exceeds the induced-investment coefficient.

stem: A farmer owns100 units of rice, consumes some and sells the rest for vegetables. If rice price rises with vegetable price fixed, how does his budget line change?
answer: A:Rotates outward about the unchanged rice-axis intercept.
solution: Let consumptions ber,v. The endowment budget isp_rr+p_vv=100p_r, orv=(p_r/p_v)(100−r). The rice intercept is always100, while the vegetable intercept100p_r/p_v rises withp_r. Thus the line rotates outward around the rice endowment point.
hint: Account for the higher value of the rice endowment as well as its price.

stem: A new firm sells50000 of output and carries7000 of unsold finished goods into next year. It buys30000 of intermediate goods, of which2000 remain unused. Find value added.
solution: Output produced is sales plus finished-goods inventory increase50000+7000=57000. Intermediate goods actually used cost30000−2000=28000; the unused stock is not current intermediate consumption. Value added is57000−28000=29000.
hint: Measure production rather than sales, and input use rather than purchases.
notes: Visual inspection confirms salesRs50000, notRs60000 from broken extraction.

stem: An economy has100 labour units and1000 capital units. Each output unit needs.5 labour and4 capital. Every household’sAPC=MPC1/2. What autonomous expenditure sustains maximum feasible output?
solution: The production limit ismin(100/.5,1000/4)=min(200,250)=200, with labour binding. Aggregate consumption isY/2. AtY200, planned expenditureY/2+A equalsY only ifA100. Equivalently, multiplier2 times autonomous expenditure100 generates200.
hint: Find the binding factor capacity before applying the multiplier.

stem: A competitive firm pays output taxt and has costC(q,k)+K, withC_k<0,C_q>0,C_qq>0. If efficiency parameterk rises whilet is fixed, what is necessarily true?
solution: Profit isπ=(P−t)q−C(q,k)−K. Keeping the old quantity fixed, higherk lowers variable cost becauseC_k<0, increasing profit; reoptimization cannot reduce that gain. At a regular interior optimum the envelope theorem givesdπ*/dk=−C_k>0. The output response depends onC_qk, not specified, so total taxtq may rise or fall. Lower total cost does not by itself imply a lower marginal cost at every quantity.
hint: Use the old feasible output as a comparison, or apply the envelope theorem.

stem: In a sealed-bid second-price(Vickrey) auction the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. A painting is worth20000 to you. What should you bid?
solution: Truthful bidding is weakly dominant with private values and standard quasilinear payoffs. If the highest rival bid is below20000, winning at that rival price gives positive surplus and bidding20000 wins. If it is above20000, winning would give negative surplus and bidding20000 loses. Misreporting can only switch a desirable win to a loss or an undesirable loss to a win; it does not lower the price conditional on already winning.
hint: Your own bid controls whether you win, not the price paid conditional on winning.

stem: A person earnsY only in period1, savesS and consumes allS plus interest in period2. If the return rises from10% to12%, what happens to saving?
answer: D:It may rise, fall or stay unchanged.
solution: Higher interest makes future consumption cheaper relative to current consumption, creating a substitution effect toward saving, but also makes a given retirement target cheaper to finance, creating an opposing income effect. Their net strength depends on preferences. Log utility gives a fixed saving share independent ofr. In theCRRA two-period model with only first-period income, saving increases for relative-risk-aversionθ<1 and decreases forθ>1. Thus each listed response is possible.
hint: Interest changes both intertemporal prices and the value of future purchasing power.

stem: Fill the blanks: In standard macroeconomic goods and money markets, ___ interest affects investment and consumption, while ___ interest affects real money demand.
solution: Investment and intertemporal consumption depend on the purchasing-power return, the real interest r≈i−expected inflation. Holding non-interest-bearing money instead of interest-bearing assets sacrifices the nominal interesti, so nominal interest is the opportunity cost entering real money demand.
hint: Distinguish purchasing-power borrowing cost from the opportunity cost of cash.
